Cross-lingual transfer analysis

Which language-level features govern how well mathematical reasoning transfers out of English? This implements the GLMM from analysis.md, from the raw instance table through to the fitted model, with inspection at each stage.

knitr::opts_chunk$set(warning = FALSE, message = TRUE)

library(nanoparquet)
## Warning: package 'nanoparquet' was built under R version 4.5.2
library(dplyr)
## 
## Attaching package: 'dplyr'
## The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
## 
##     filter, lag
## The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
## 
##     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(stringr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

transfer_dir <- "../../artifacts/transfer_tables"
out_dir <- "../../artifacts/analysis"
dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

Configuration

SPLIT <- "synthetic" # "original" for the robustness check

# Excluded by base name (before the reasoning suffix), so each entry catches all
# of a model's reasoning variants.
#   gpt-5.4-nano - proprietary: no parameter count, closed tokenizer (so no
#                  fertility). Cannot enter a model with size or fertility terms.
# Granite and Olmo-3 (excluded earlier) are back in: they are reasoning-capable,
# which the reasoning section below needs. Granite adds a non-Qwen on/off pair;
# Olmo-3-7B-Think is reasoning-on only in the synthetic split.
EXCLUDED_MODELS <- c(
  "gpt-5.4-nano"
)

# eng_metric is English with metric units, not a language, and has no typological
# or resource features. uncorrected_isl is machine-translated Icelandic before
# human correction, kept in the dataset for the validation figure but not used in
# the analysis. English itself is kept -- it anchors the intercept at fertility 1,
# typological distance 0, maximum resource.
EXCLUDED_LANGUAGES <- c("eng_metric", "uncorrected_isl")

Load the instance table

collect_transfer_tables.py writes one Parquet row per evaluated instance: correct as a logical, the reasoning mode in the model name, and every feature we need – typological_distance, log10_common_crawl_pages, and the tokenizer fertilities. Normalised fertility is the model’s fertility relative to its own English fertility, so there are no separate feature tables to join.

observations <- read_parquet(file.path(transfer_dir, "analysis.parquet")) %>%
  select(
    source_id, language, correct, model, family, params_b, split, eval_id,
    typological_distance, log10_common_crawl_pages,
    tokenizer_fertility, english_fertility_tokens_per_character
  ) %>%
  mutate(normalized_fertility = tokenizer_fertility / english_fertility_tokens_per_character)

dim(observations)
## [1] 813782     13

Reasoning mode

Reasoning mode is explicit in the model name. Qwen3 / Qwen3.5 label the reasoning-on default with a bare name and only suffix (reasoning off); granite and Olmo-3 label both sides. We give every reasoning-split model a consistent (reasoning on) / (reasoning off) label and derive base_model (the tokenizer identity, shared across modes) by stripping it.

# Bases that appear with a "(reasoning off)" variant: their bare form is the
# reasoning-on run and should be labelled as such.
off_bases <- observations %>%
  filter(str_detect(model, "\\(reasoning off\\)$")) %>%
  mutate(base = str_remove(model, "\\s*\\(reasoning off\\)$")) %>%
  distinct(base) %>%
  pull(base)

observations <- observations %>%
  mutate(
    model = if_else(model %in% off_bases, paste0(model, " (reasoning on)"), model),
    base_model = str_remove(model, "\\s*\\(reasoning (on|off)\\)$")
  )

observations %>%
  filter(base_model %in% off_bases) %>%
  distinct(base_model, model) %>%
  arrange(base_model)
## # A data frame: 26 × 2
##    base_model      model                          
##    <chr>           <chr>                          
##  1 Olmo-3-7B-Think Olmo-3-7B-Think (reasoning off)
##  2 Olmo-3-7B-Think Olmo-3-7B-Think (reasoning on) 
##  3 Qwen3-0.6B      Qwen3-0.6B (reasoning off)     
##  4 Qwen3-0.6B      Qwen3-0.6B (reasoning on)      
##  5 Qwen3-1.7B      Qwen3-1.7B (reasoning off)     
##  6 Qwen3-1.7B      Qwen3-1.7B (reasoning on)      
##  7 Qwen3-14B       Qwen3-14B (reasoning off)      
##  8 Qwen3-14B       Qwen3-14B (reasoning on)       
##  9 Qwen3-32B       Qwen3-32B (reasoning off)      
## 10 Qwen3-32B       Qwen3-32B (reasoning on)

Filter to the analysis set

EXCLUDED_MODELS is matched on base_model, so it catches every reasoning variant of a listed model.

observations <- observations %>%
  filter(
    split == SPLIT,
    !language %in% EXCLUDED_LANGUAGES,
    !base_model %in% EXCLUDED_MODELS
  )

count(observations, language)

Feature coverage

Every feature is present for every included cell; the only rows the parquet leaves without features are the ones we already drop (gpt-5.4-nano has no tokenizer fertility, eng_metric no language features).

observations %>%
  summarise(across(
    c(typological_distance, log10_common_crawl_pages, normalized_fertility),
    ~ sum(is.na(.)), .names = "na_{.col}"
  ))
##   na_typological_distance na_log10_common_crawl_pages na_normalized_fertility
## 1                       0                           0                       0

Aggregate to cells

One row per (model, language, template). Every predictor is constant within such a cell, so Binomial(n_total, pi) has the same likelihood as the individual Bernoulli draws at roughly 1/28th the rows – carried through with first().

cells <- observations %>%
  group_by(model, family, language, template = source_id) %>%
  summarise(
    n_correct = sum(correct),
    n_total = n(),
    params_b = first(params_b),
    typological_distance_from_english = first(typological_distance),
    log10_common_crawl_pages = first(log10_common_crawl_pages),
    normalized_fertility = first(normalized_fertility),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

dim(cells)
## [1] 31500    10
summary(cells$n_total)
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##   20.00   20.00   20.00   20.19   20.00   40.00

n_total is 20 per cell except for OLMo-2-0425-1B-Instruct in dan, eng and nob, where a duplicate evaluation run doubles it to 40. Those two runs are one configuration sampled twice (near-identical accuracy, same instance ids), so pooling them slightly overstates precision for three cells of one model; refitting without them moved no coefficient materially. Left pooled here pending an upstream dedup in collect_transfer_tables.py.

The design is otherwise balanced – every model seen in every language, 100 templates each:

Predictors

Standardise the continuous predictors so the interaction terms are interpretable at the mean and the weakly-informative priors are on a sensible scale.

standardise <- function(x) as.numeric((x - mean(x)) / sd(x))

cells <- cells %>%
  mutate(
    log2_params = log2(params_b),
    fertility_z = standardise(normalized_fertility),
    typological_distance_z = standardise(typological_distance_from_english),
    log_resource_z = standardise(log10_common_crawl_pages),
    log_params_z = standardise(log2_params),
    # base_model is the tokenizer/weights identity shared across reasoning modes;
    # reasoning is the on/off knob (non-reasoning models are "off"). Used below.
    base_model = str_remove(model, "\\s*\\(reasoning (on|off)\\)$"),
    reasoning = factor(if_else(str_detect(model, "\\(reasoning on\\)$"), "on", "off"), levels = c("off", "on"))
  ) %>%
  arrange(family, model, language, template)

cells %>%
  select(fertility_z, typological_distance_z, log_resource_z, log_params_z) %>%
  summary()
##   fertility_z       typological_distance_z log_resource_z     log_params_z

##  1st Qu.:-0.60747   1st Qu.:-0.4250        1st Qu.:-0.7574   1st Qu.:-0.8296

##  Max.   : 4.41150   Max.   : 1.9009        Max.   : 1.4472   Max.   : 2.0064

Two of these are language-level, so their main effects rest on 7 points regardless of the 566k instances behind them. Worth seeing the collinearity before reading any coefficient:

cells %>%
  select(fertility_z, typological_distance_z, log_resource_z, log_params_z) %>%
  cor() %>%
  round(2)
##                        fertility_z typological_distance_z log_resource_z
## fertility_z                   1.00                   0.81          -0.04
## typological_distance_z        0.81                   1.00          -0.13
## log_resource_z               -0.04                  -0.13           1.00
## log_params_z                  0.00                   0.00           0.00
##                        log_params_z
## fertility_z                       0
## typological_distance_z            0
## log_resource_z                    0
## log_params_z                      1

Fertility and typological distance are strongly related, so their individual coefficients should not be read independently.

cells %>%
  distinct(model, language, normalized_fertility, typological_distance_from_english, log10_common_crawl_pages) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(normalized_fertility, typological_distance_from_english, log10_common_crawl_pages)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(value, language)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~name, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Feature spread across languages") +
  theme_minimal()

Raw accuracy by language and size, as a sanity check on what the model should recover.

Languages are ordered by resource level and coloured on a sequential ramp rather than with categorical hues: resource is a magnitude, so the colour should carry the ordering. mako runs dark to light through a single blue-green hue, is monotonic in lightness (so the order survives greyscale and colour-vision deficiency), and avoids the pale yellow end of viridis that disappears against a white panel. Highest-resource language is darkest.

language_levels <- cells %>%
  distinct(language, log10_common_crawl_pages) %>%
  arrange(desc(log10_common_crawl_pages))

# Label with the resource value so the legend states the ordering explicitly.
language_labels <- sprintf("%s (%.1f)", language_levels$language, language_levels$log10_common_crawl_pages)
names(language_labels) <- language_levels$language

language_levels
## # A tibble: 7 × 2
##   language log10_common_crawl_pages
##   <chr>                       <dbl>
## 1 eng                          8.95
## 2 rus                          8.14
## 3 deu                          8.11
## 4 zho                          8.01
## 5 dan                          7.06
## 6 nob                          6.85
## 7 isl                          5.89
cells %>%
  group_by(model, language, log2_params) %>%
  summarise(accuracy = sum(n_correct) / sum(n_total), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(language = factor(language, levels = language_levels$language)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(log2_params, accuracy, colour = language)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.85, size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(
    option = "mako", begin = 0.08, end = 0.82, direction = 1,
    labels = language_labels
  ) +
  # loess is unconstrained and overshoots 1.0 at the top end; clip the view
  # rather than the data so the smoother still sees every point.
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    x = "log2 parameters (B)", y = "accuracy",
    colour = expression(Language ~ (log[10] ~ CC ~ pages)),
    title = "Transfer gap narrows with scale",
    subtitle = "Languages ordered by resource level, darkest = highest resource"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

Model

Language features are model-by-language (fertility) or language-only (typological distance, resource). Interacting them with size tests the claim that scale governs how much of the transfer gap survives.

The baseline drops the language features and keeps size; the quantity of interest is how far sd(model:language) shrinks between the two, i.e. how much of the cross-lingual transfer variation the language features explain.

This document fits the model with lme4, keeping template and family as random effects (the model as written in analysis.md) – glmer handles them quickly. The Bayesian counterpart in transfer_brms.Rmd makes those two fixed instead, purely for sampling geometry (as random effects the template SD funnels and the single-model family, Apertus, makes a flat ridge that saturates the NUTS treedepth); sd(model:language), the quantity of interest, is the same either way.

We save the prepared cells so the Bayesian document reads them directly rather than re-running the 786k-row prep.

cells <- cells %>% mutate(across(c(model, base_model, family, language, template), as.factor))
saveRDS(cells, file.path(out_dir, "model_cells.rds"))

script (shared vs. not) from analysis.md is deliberately absent. With only zho and rus non-Latin out of 7 languages it is nearly collinear with typological distance and not separately identifiable – report it descriptively instead.

lme4

glmer wants cbind(successes, failures) rather than brms’ trials() syntax. The baseline drops the language features; comparing its sd(model:language) to the full model’s is how we read off the transfer variance the features explain.

library(lme4)
## Loading required package: Matrix
## 
## Attaching package: 'Matrix'
## The following objects are masked from 'package:tidyr':
## 
##     expand, pack, unpack
random_effects <- "(1 | family / model) + (1 | template) + (1 | model:language)"

fit_baseline <- glmer(
  as.formula(paste("cbind(n_correct, n_total - n_correct) ~ log_params_z +", random_effects)),
  data = cells, family = binomial()
)
fit_full <- glmer(
  as.formula(paste(
    "cbind(n_correct, n_total - n_correct) ~",
    "(fertility_z + typological_distance_z + log_resource_z) * log_params_z +", random_effects
  )),
  data = cells, family = binomial()
)

summary(fit_full)

)

Analysis of results

KCE: the following is a work in progress

We see that size have the largest effect of parameters, with larger models performing (1.94, p<0.05) secondly see that higher resource languages leads to a higher performance (.699, p<0.05), but that the effect is less pronounced for larger models (-.210, p<0.05). Language with a higher typological distance from English, generally leads to worse performance (-.299, p<0.05) and higher tokenizer fertility improved the likelihood of obtaining the correct answer (.193, p<0.05).

The interactions between tokenizer fertility and the model size (-.0576, p=.423), and between typological distance and model size (.0332, p=.634) where not found to be significant, indicating that effect of fertility and language distance remains a problem regardless of the size (or at least we couldn’t detect if it was influenced by it).

Beyond the individual coefficients we can ask how much of the cross-lingual transfer these language features account for. The model-by-language random effect captures how much a model’s accuracy in a given language departs from its overall skill and the template difficulty – the transfer variation the fixed effects leave unexplained. Adding the three language features shrinks this variance component from \(\sigma^2 = 1.10\) (SD 1.05) in the size-only baseline to \(\sigma^2 = 0.39\) (SD 0.63) in the full model, a 64% reduction in variance (40% on the SD scale). Roughly two-thirds of the transfer variation that remains after accounting for model skill and template difficulty is thus captured by tokenizer fertility, typological distance and resource level together.

Questions:

  • Is it a difference in parsing or “reasoning”
  • is there more of the variance that could be explained?
  • there is high correlation between fertility and language distance (estionian might fix it).
    • One potential solution it to decompose into fertility across model (fertility between), this should be colinear to typoligical distance, while the model devisation from the langauge mean fertility (fertility within) would be orthogonal
  • add bootstrap on proportion of variance explained (for later)
    • potentially some systematicity, but hard to say with only 7 languages
      • non-linearity in resource: It seems to overreport on low-resource languages and underreport on high-resource (we could apply non-linearity to resourcity)
      • Chinese is likely an outlier (estimates of resourcity is likely incorrect for some of the models, e.g. Qwen)

Note when writing: there are three actionable parameters, fertility, model size and reasoning, but depending these might have varying effects on downstream languages.

Exploratory: does more structure help?

Two additions the questions above point to, each refitting the full model with one extra term.

A resource x typological-distance interaction. It is significant but a minor lever – variance explained moves 64.4% to 65.9%. The coefficient is positive, so a high resource level buffers the typological-distance penalty: distance hurts less when there is more data for the language.

fit_rxt <- update(fit_full, . ~ . + typological_distance_z:log_resource_z)

anova(fit_full, fit_rxt)
## Data: cells
## Models:
## fit_full: cbind(n_correct, n_total - n_correct) ~ (fertility_z + typological_distance_z + log_resource_z) * log_params_z + (1 | family/model) + (1 | template) + (1 | model:language)
## fit_rxt: cbind(n_correct, n_total - n_correct) ~ fertility_z + typological_distance_z + log_resource_z + log_params_z + (1 | family/model) + (1 | template) + (1 | model:language) + fertility_z:log_params_z + typological_distance_z:log_params_z + log_resource_z:log_params_z + typological_distance_z:log_resource_z
##          npar    AIC    BIC logLik -2*log(L)  Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq)    
## fit_full   12 188494 188594 -94235    188470

summary(fit_rxt)$coefficients["typological_distance_z:log_resource_z", , drop = FALSE]
##                                        Estimate Std. Error  z value
## typological_distance_z:log_resource_z 0.4400338  0.1167123 3.770243
##                                           Pr(>|z|)
## typological_distance_z:log_resource_z 0.0001630887

A per-language residual (1 | language). Strongly significant, with sd(language) ~ 0.42: roughly half of the transfer variation the three features leave unexplained is systematic per-language structure, not model-by-language idiosyncrasy – i.e. there are language features still to add. The random-effect estimates show which languages the features over- or under-predict, a starting point for “which languages do we transfer to poorly”.

fit_lang <- update(fit_full, . ~ . + (1 | language))

anova(fit_full, fit_lang)

Reasoning

Reasoning is a model-level knob you can actually turn, so it gets its own model. The reasoning-capable models are run both ways – Qwen3-8B (reasoning on) vs (reasoning off) – a within-base paired design, so the effect is identified within base_model (12 paired base models across Granite, Qwen3 and Qwen3.5; Olmo-3-7B-Think is reasoning-on only, so it contributes no pair). We add reasoning as a fixed effect and interact it with the language features and size, to ask not just whether reasoning helps but whether it narrows the transfer gap.

fit_reasoning <- glmer(
  cbind(n_correct, n_total - n_correct) ~
    (fertility_z + typological_distance_z + log_resource_z) * log_params_z +
    reasoning * (fertility_z + typological_distance_z + log_resource_z + log_params_z) +
    (1 | family / base_model) + (1 | template) + (1 | model:language),
  data = cells, family = binomial()
)

round(summary(fit_reasoning)$coefficients, 4)
##                                     Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
## (Intercept)                           0.0652     0.4930  0.1323   0.8947
## fertility_z                           0.1077     0.0908  1.1854   0.2359
## typological_distance_z               -0.2515     0.0912 -2.7575   0.0058
## log_resource_z                        0.7889     0.0516 15.2813   0.0000
## log_params_z                          1.7900     0.1945  9.2024   0.0000
## reasoningon                           0.3032     0.1177  2.5749   0.0100
## fertility_z:log_params_z             -0.0539     0.0834 -0.6462   0.5182
## typological_distance_z:log_params_z   0.0344     0.0787  0.4371   0.6620
## log_resource_z:log_params_z          -0.2092     0.0438 -4.7770   0.0000
## fertility_z:reasoningon               0.4289     0.1787  2.3997   0.0164
## typological_distance_z:reasoningon   -0.2811     0.1722 -1.6325   0.1026
## log_resource_z:reasoningon           -0.1888     0.0961 -1.9642   0.0495
## log_params_z:reasoningon              0.2829     0.1200  2.3588   0.0183

Reasoning raises accuracy (reasoningon ~ +0.30 logit, p ~ .01). More useful for transfer, the resource advantage shrinks under reasoning (log_resource_z:reasoningon ~ -0.19, p ~ .05): reasoning helps lower-resource languages relatively more, so it is a lever that narrows the resource-driven gap. Reasoning also interacts with size (log_params_z:reasoningon ~ +0.28, p ~ .02) – larger models gain more on the logit scale, though small models can gain more in raw accuracy because large models sit near the ceiling. The fertility and typological-distance interactions with reasoning are entangled by their mutual collinearity, as for the main effects, and are not separately identifiable here.
